sections.section_title: The Argument from Their Own Experience
sections.summary: Paul argues from an event the Galatians can attest without consulting anyone -- that they received the Spirit, and still experience it, by a hearing of faith rather than by works of law -- and asks whether something begun in the Spirit is now being completed by flesh, i.e. by circumcision.
sections.relevance: The reading treats enarchomai/epiteleo as a matched pair naming the inauguration and completion of a single process, so what is at stake is not an optional extra but the medium in which the thing they already have is brought to its end. Verse 4 then raises the possibility that everything they experienced has come to nothing -- and the neutral reading stresses that Paul retracts the assertion mid-sentence ('if indeed it really was in vain'), which holds the outcome open rather than settling it either way. That the possibility of forfeiture is raised at all, of people who demonstrably possess the Spirit, bears on the question; that Paul declines to assert it, and that his subject is the basis on which the Spirit came rather than the tenure of anyone's standing, keeps this short of a direct argument about permanence.
key_phrases: Having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by flesh?
Did you experience so many things in vain -- if indeed it was in vain?
did you receive the Spirit by works of law or by a hearing of faith?

sections.summary: Paul answers the question of who counts as Abraham's offspring by going behind Genesis 17 to Genesis 15, where Abraham is reckoned righteous by believing before any covenant sign exists, and by citing the promise's own stated scope -- that all the nations would be blessed in him.
sections.relevance: The reading shows righteousness here is entered on Abraham's side of a ledger (logizomai, a bookkeeping word) on the basis of believing, at a point when the rite now being urged on the Galatians did not yet exist -- so the basis of standing is detached from performance of a marker, which is the ground on which permanence is usually argued. Cutting the other way, the group is named by a present characteristic (hoi ek pisteos, 'those whose defining derivation is faith'), and the blessing is described as shared with Abraham rather than transferred, so the passage identifies who stands rather than stating how long they stand. It settles the basis of standing, not its duration.
key_phrases: believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness
those of faith, these are sons of Abraham
those of faith are blessed along with Abraham, the man of faith

sections.summary: Paul sets four scriptural citations against one another -- the summary curse of Deuteronomy 27:26, Habakkuk 2:4, Leviticus 18:5 and Deuteronomy 21:23 -- to argue that Christ redeemed 'us' out of the law's specific curse so that the Abrahamic blessing might reach the Gentiles and 'we' receive the promised Spirit.
sections.relevance: Conventionally 3:10-13 is cited to prove that no one can keep the law, so that standing must rest on a finished substitutionary transaction and therefore cannot be forfeited. The neutral reading shows the passage is doing something else. The verse Paul quotes is the closing summary curse of a covenant-sanctions document about national infidelity, not a statement about human capacity, and the reading lays out three candidate premises for 3:10 and finds the familiar 'nobody keeps it' premise the weakest of the three -- held against Deuteronomy 30:11-14 in the same covenant block, Paul's own 'blameless' at Philippians 3:6, Luke 1:6, and the Torah's own atonement provisions. What is redeemed is stated precisely as 'the curse of the law,' the specific curse of verse 10, not a condition in general; and the pronoun seam in verse 14 shows what arrives among the Gentiles is the older Abrahamic blessing rather than a release from that curse. The passage is thus about a covenantal and historical transaction and the promise's arrival among the nations, not about whether an individual's standing, once given, can be lost.
key_phrases: Cursed is everyone who does not abide by all things written in the book of the law
Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us
so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles
the righteous shall live by faith

sections.summary: Arguing from ordinary legal practice, Paul holds that a ratified diatheke cannot be annulled or have a codicil added to it, so the law arriving 430 years later cannot invalidate the promise made to Abraham and his offspring, and the inheritance therefore runs on promise rather than on law.
sections.relevance: This is the chapter's strongest permanence language: kekyromene ('ratified,' an instrument that has taken effect), ou akyroi ('does not un-validate'), and an inheritance (kleronomia) described by the reading as something received because of who one is rather than something earned. Its bearing is limited in a specific way the reading insists on: the argument is about priority and irrevocability between two instruments -- what a later arrangement can do to an earlier one -- not about whether a named heir can forfeit his share, and the reading explicitly rules out reading it as a claim about rank. So it asserts that the promise itself is unrevisable without saying anything about the tenure of those who hold under it.
key_phrases: once it has been ratified, no one annuls it or adds a codicil to it
does not annul a covenant previously ratified by God, so as to void the promise
if the inheritance is by law, it is no longer by promise

sections.summary: Paul accounts for Sinai as an addition made because of transgressions with a stated terminus, denies that the law stands against God's promises, and states in a contrary-to-fact conditional that no law able to make alive was ever given, so that the promise is given to those who believe.
sections.relevance: The reading presses that 3:21 is a claim about the law's remit rather than about human performance under it -- 'no law able to make alive was given' is a different proposition from 'a law was given that nobody managed to keep' -- and that the sentence is a defence of the law, not an indictment. That removes performance from the account of how life is had at all: it is given (dothe) on promise. The bearing on permanence is indirect, since the passage is about salvation-historical function rather than about anyone's tenure, and the recipients are named with a present participle, tois pisteuousin, 'those who believe.'
key_phrases: if a law had been given that was able to make alive, then righteousness would indeed have been by law
it was added because of transgressions, until the offspring should come
so that the promise by faith of Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe

sections.summary: Paul describes a period of custody under law that ran until faith came, using the household image of the paidagogos -- a slave who escorted a boy to school and whose term ended by the calendar at the boy's majority, not for any failure on his part -- and states that 'we' are no longer under that supervision.

Paul tells the Galatian congregations that they are all sons of God through faith, that those baptized into Christ have put on Christ, that the three pairs of distinctions do not obtain within that sphere, and that belonging to Christ makes them Abraham's offspring and heirs according to promise.
sections.relevance: Standing is stated here as a present, accomplished fact in the strongest terms the chapter has -- Israel's own family language applied to Gentiles, investiture in Christ as a garment one is thereafter dealt with as wearing, and a community described with heis, one masculine singular person. The reading finds that what the three-pair formula denies is the bearing of those categories on standing within the sphere named, which removes the markers by which standing might otherwise be earned or lost. The counterweight is the form of verse 29: the whole qualification is an ei clause, 'if you are Christ's' -- though the reading takes that as identifying the class (belonging to Christ, with no rite in the answer) rather than as raising the prospect of ceasing to belong. It states the basis and the fact of the standing; it does not state its duration.
key_phrases: you are all sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus
as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ
you are all one in Christ Jesus
if you are Christ's, then you are Abraham's offspring, heirs according to promise
